prompt.en: A daytime forecast raises the LUF on a path from 4 MHz to 7 MHz while the MUF remains near 18 MHz. What should happen to a 5.3 MHz plan compared with a 14.2 MHz plan?

text.en: Both plans improve equally because a higher LUF makes every HF frequency more usable.
The 5.3 MHz plan moves from inside the old window to below the new lower edge, while 14.2 MHz remains inside.
The 14.2 MHz plan fails first because D-region absorption is always worse at higher HF.
Both plans must move to 18 MHz because every usable choice equals the upper limit.

explanation.en: Before the change, 5.3 MHz was above the 4 MHz LUF. After the LUF rises to 7 MHz, it is below the usable window. A 14.2 MHz signal remains between 7 and 18 MHz, so it is still a plausible path choice.

prompt.en: A forecast gives an afternoon MUF of 22 MHz for a path. If the operator uses an 85% OWF planning estimate, which target is closest?

explanation.en: Multiplying 22 MHz by 0.85 gives 18.7 MHz. OWF is a practical choice below the MUF, not at or above it.

prompt.en: A straight-up ionosonde test and a shallow long-distance path use the same F region. Why can the shallow path work at a higher frequency than the vertical test?

text.en: The shallow path needs less bending to return to Earth.
The shallow path spends more time in the D region, so absorption becomes useful.
The vertical test ignores sunlight, while the shallow path creates ionization by itself.
The path frequency limit rises because transmitter power changes the critical frequency.

explanation.en: Critical frequency is a vertical test. At a shallow angle, less bending is needed to return the wave, so the path MUF can be higher than the vertical critical frequency.
